high.title: intent:// URL launched without clearing its component and selector
high.description: Intent.parseUri() turns a URL into an Intent that is then started, and this file does not call both setComponent(null) and setSelector(null) on it. The app implements an Intent redirection vulnerability in its WebView client. It parses URLs starting with 'intent://' using Intent.parseUri() and calls startActivity() on the resulting Intent. While there is a check for a specific action and package on line 18, the 'else' block on line 22 still proceeds to start the parsed Intent regardless of whether it matched the allowlist, allowing a remote attacker to launch any activity on the device by tricking the user into visiting a malicious URL.
high.impact: A web page or link that reaches this code names any activity in the app - exported or not - with extras of its choosing, the classic WebView-to-private-component jump.

intent.putExtra("info", "Sensitive information");
android.util.Log.d(TAG, "intent action = " + intent.getAction());
webView.getContext().startActivity(intent);

high.recommendation: After parseUri(), call setComponent(null), setSelector(null) and addCategory(BROWSABLE), or launch only intents whose target is on an allowlist.

low.title: Exported activity DisplayActivity has no permission protection
low.description: Activity "edu.ksu.cs.benign.DisplayActivity" is reachable by any app on the device (Has an intent-filter and no explicit android:exported (implicitly exported)) and declares no permission. It handles DISP. Deep-link schemes: benign. DisplayActivity is exported and accessible to any third-party app without requiring a permission.
low.impact: Another app can launch this activity and potentially leak data or manipulate its UI, although the impact here is limited to displaying error messages provided in the intent.
low.recommendation: Set android:exported="false" if it is internal, or guard it with a signature-level permission and validate all input.

reasons: The described impact is limited to displaying attacker-provided error messages, which does not justify a Medium severity.

info.title: Missing screenshot protection
info.description: The app does not set FLAG_SECURE on its activities.
info.impact: Sensitive information displayed on the screen can be captured via screenshots or screen recording apps.
info.recommendation: Call getWindow().setFlags(WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE, WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE) in the onCreate() of sensitive activities.

reasons: Screen contents not protected from capture. Without FLAG_SECURE, what a screen shows can end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview. That matters on screens showing credentials, card numbers or balances; on its own it is a hardening note.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The app declares neither android:networkSecurityConfig nor usesCleartextTraffic, so it relies on platform defaults and pins no domain. With targetSdkVersion 27 those defaults still permit cleartext HTTP (see the cleartext finding).
info.impact: Without pinning, anyone who gets a CA trusted on the device can read and alter the app's TLS traffic.
info.recommendation: Declare a network security config that disables cleartext and pins the domains that carry sensitive traffic.

reasons: No certificate pinning. Pinning defends against an attacker who already controls a trusted CA or the device's trust store. Without one of those, TLS is still doing its job. It becomes a finding when paired with what the unpinned channel actually carries.
The absence of pinning is a hardening note that only becomes a vulnerability when paired with a finding showing sensitive data on the channel.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 allows implicit component export
info.description: On targetSdk 27, any component with an intent-filter is exported unless it says otherwise.
info.recommendation: Raise targetSdkVersion to 31+ and declare android:exported explicitly on every filtered component.

reasons: Legacy platform behaviour from SDK levels. An SDK level is a statement about which platform defaults apply, not a defect. It is context for the findings that depend on those defaults - pair it with one of them.
This is documented platform behavior for the target SDK; it provides the context for findings like Exported activity DisplayActivity has no permission protection.
warnings: Implicit export only applies below targetSdk 31; confirm the app's targetSdkVersion before treating this as exploitable.

info.title: Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower
info.description: minSdkVersion 22 lets the app run on Android versions before 11, and its task affinity is its package name "edu.ksu.cs.benign". There, another app can declare the same affinity, with allowTaskReparenting, and have its own activity shown in this app's task. The app targets SDK 27 and does not specify android:taskAffinity, making it susceptible to task hijacking (StrandHogg) on Android 10 and lower.
info.impact: A malicious app can place its own activity on top of the app's task, potentially phishing user credentials.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to 30, where Android fixed this. Until then, android:taskAffinity="" on the <application> mitigates the original attack, though not its runtime variant on unpatched Android 9 and lower.
